articles.author: Vincent Acovino
articles.description: In video games, "barks" are short lines of dialogue given to various characters in the world. Grand Theft Auto VI proves how this kind of dialogue contributes to an immersive world.
articles.title: How non-player characters in 'Grand Theft Auto VI' help create its big world

articles.author: Mandalit del Barco
articles.description: A new movie about the making of Sylvester Stallone's 1976 film Rocky opens nationwide this week. It made him a star and helped revolutionize cinematography — including technology still used today.
articles.title: How the Steadicam sprinted up the stairs along with Rocky

articles.author: Sheldon Pearce
articles.description: Their new album makes the case for rappers Elucid and billy woods as an era-defining team: attuned to a dark sociopolitical moment, yet powered by a humans-first creative ethic.
articles.title: Armand Hammer has what it takes to outlast the end times

articles.author: Rachel Treisman
articles.description: A federal judge has twice delayed construction of Trump's arch. Another is keeping East Potomac Park open. The proposed golf course redesign got mixed feedback from a federal arts panel on Thursday.
articles.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

articles.author: Allison Aubrey
articles.description: How do we maintain healthy romantic relationships as we age? Allison Aubrey and Scott Detrow talk about about the science of healthy, later-in-life relationships.
articles.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

articles.author: Domenico Montanaro
articles.description: Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That 14-point spread is the widest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
articles.title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years

articles.author: Lorcan Lovett
articles.description: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar security forces "acted with genocidal intent" against the Rohingya during military operations in the northern Rakhine state in 2017.
articles.title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

articles.author: Marc Silver
articles.description: Yahoo for the loo! November 19 marks the 25th anniversary of World Toilet Day. The theme this year: "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures."
articles.title: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets

articles.author: Majd Al-Waheidi
articles.description: As Democrats prepare to take control of the House, incoming majority leader Katherine Clark discusses the party's ambitious agenda and divisions within its ranks.
articles.title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity

articles.author: A Martínez
articles.description: Rep. Gregory Meeks raises concerns about U.S. alliances after Trump's summit with Xi and Putin. He also discusses Chinese espionage amid the Nvidia scandal.
articles.title: Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit

articles.author: Tory Shepherd
articles.description:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives
Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme
An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.
The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges

articles.author: Penry Buckley NSW state reporter
articles.description:
Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.
In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kellie Sloane says she’s ‘pretty sure’ NSW Liberals exodus is over after Mark Speakman resigns

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic Editor
articles.description:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner
The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

articles.author: Ali Aziz, Maria Talal and Tom Levitt
articles.description:
Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists
The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests

articles.author: Matthew Weaver
articles.description:
Exclusive: Investigation launched after details of grief and trauma uploaded, raising questions over extent of issue
The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers.
Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff

articles.author: Kat Wong
articles.description:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon’s explanations of body disposal ‘ring hollow’, court hears

articles.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
articles.description:
Public expectations around datacentres have changed in the age of AI, chief executive Craig Scroggie says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.
The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NextDC vows to keep future datacentres away from homes after community backlash in Melbourne

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Jury convicts Raelene Polymiadis after four-month trial in South Australian supreme court

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A jury has convicted a diabetic woman of murdering both her elderly parents with insulin after a marathon criminal trial.
Raelene Polymiadis, 66, will face two mandatory life sentences after jurors on Friday delivered unanimous verdicts after a four-month South Australian supreme court trial.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Perfect weapon’: diabetic woman found guilty of murdering her 94-year-old parents with insulin

articles.author: Auzzy Byrdsell
articles.description:
Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail
Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fiona the hippo dies after ingesting knitted hat at Cincinnati zoo

articles.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Polly Hudson, produced by Ruth Abrahams, Saskia Collette, Eleanor Biggs, Harriet Mogie and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
After Russell Brand’s conviction and accusations against David Walliams, campaigners are calling for a staggered age of consent. Nosheen Iqbal speaks to the columnist Polly Hudson and the educator Michael Conroy about what needs to change
Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com
Anger, disgust, shame. In the last couple of weeks, as news of famous older men being convicted and accused of crimes against very young women and girls has emerged, the public mood has shifted.
The conversation has moved from “how did society let this happen?” to “how do we stop it from happening again?”. In that space, a campaign has grown for the consent gap to be closed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is it time to change the UK age of consent? – podcast

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Marina Dunbar and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other, according to the New York Times.
The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors.
A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.
The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role.
The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December. Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.
Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump administration asks federal court to dismiss its lawsuit over US Senate election in Alaska – as it happened

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Dennes, 70, was convicted of killing a Houston jeweler, and groaned for an hour after pentobarbital was administered
Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying a lethal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative.
Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the US on Thursday, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Texas botches execution of Reinaldo Dennes as staffers struggle to find vein

articles.author: Robert Mackey
articles.description:
President had sought to block results if Democrat won race that featured two candidates named Dan Sullivan
In a legal filing on Thursday, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the midterm elections seeking to block the certification of the US Senate race in Alaska should Democrat Mary Peltola win.
The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska supreme court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was legal and that he could be on the ballot.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agency
articles.description:
The controlled detonation can lead to a plume containing lead particles, worrying residents and state officials
The US army has delayed its plan to detonate a stash of bomb-making chemicals in south-eastern Iowa as questions swirl about the public health risks.
The army was set to blow up about 5 tons of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, at noon on Friday, a move it described as the safest way to dispose of the highly sensitive compound.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US army postpones plan to detonate bomb-making chemical amid outcry

articles.author: By Associated Press
articles.description:
Judge in Florida says an expert has determined the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex is mentally competent to face charges
An expert has determined that Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California, a judge said on Thursday.
Markle’s defense lawyer said they would not contest the finding by Dr Amie Gerodimos. The exam was ordered after his arrest at a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, on 6 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, is competent to face child sex abuse images case

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Hotly anticipated Bonnie and Clyde-inspired adventure GTA VI has gamers glued to their screens around the world
Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.
GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment

articles.author: Rajeev Syal and Lisa O’Carroll
articles.description:
Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

articles.author: Jakub Krupa (now) and Hamish Mackay (earlier)
articles.description:
Berlin meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting with Xi in China
For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media, includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.
There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:
“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine allies warn ‘Yalta format’ will not bring about peace – as it happened

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey; produced by Annie La Vespa; music by Axel Kacoutié; executive producer Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China. Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity?
You can read Pippa Crerar’s article on the EU’s approach to a reset with the UK here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast

articles.author: Julian Borger
articles.description:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.
In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

articles.author: Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen
articles.description:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

articles.author: Ariana Baio
articles.description:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China

articles.author: Kaamil Ahmed in The Hague and Yassin Abdumonab in Cox's Bazar
articles.description:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world
There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.
But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote

articles.author: Kaamil Ahmed in The Hague, and Oliver Holmes
articles.description:
Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes
Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

UK politics live – latest updates


The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

articles.author: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem
articles.description:
First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu
The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza

articles.author: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Arab MPs accuse politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards Palestinians at four locations in Kafr Qasim
Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.
Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eight injured after driver in Israel repeatedly rams car into Palestinians

articles.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
articles.description:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport
Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas  
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president

articles.author: Tom Phillips Latin America correspondent
articles.description:
Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military

articles.author: Tom Ambrose (now); Taz Ali and Kate Lamb (earlier)
articles.description:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.
It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu
Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.
Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

articles.author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
articles.description:
St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access
The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

articles.author: Imran Lodhi, as told to Morgan Krakow
articles.description:
When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story
Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan
Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

articles.title: ‘I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl buried in mud. I knew we had to do something’ – This is climate breakdown

Democrats who might be thinking of launching a presidential run in 2028 are starting to make moves. One such contender is Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary under Joe Biden. Is he the candidate who can unite the broad church in his party?

articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other, according to the New York Times.
The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors.
A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.
The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role.
The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December. Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.
Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump administration asks federal court to dismiss its lawsuit over US Senate election in Alaska – as it happened

Sean Cairncross exits after outages that sparked fierce criticism, with DoD official Kirsten Davies to take over
White House national ⁠cyber director Sean ⁠Cairncross ​was ousted from his job, a person close to the White House told Reuters on Thursday, ⁠days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and ⁠strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense chief information officer ​Kirsten Davies will ‌assume the position ‌temporarily, according to the source.

articles.description:
Rose pleaded guilty to tax evasion in 1990

Player also banned from baseball over bets

Donald Trump says he has posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR + LEGEND,” Trump posted on social media.

articles.author: José Olivares
articles.description:
New Jersey congresswoman, charged with interfering with immigration arrest, set to face trial over May 2025 incident
An appeals court decided on Thursday that the Democratic New Jersey representative LaMonica McIver will continue to face charges related to a skirmish outside an immigration detention center last year when she attempted to conduct an oversight visit there.
The court’s decision to decline McIver’s request to overturn the court’s earlier ruling comes just a day after she pressed the homeland security secretary for the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operations, telling the secretary: “You are killing people.”

articles.author: Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
articles.description:
Anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear overnight. The new Congress – and all of us – must rise to the occasion
Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.
And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank

articles.author: Rachel Leingang
articles.description:
Flanagan will become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate, and hopes young Native people see themselves in her win
Peggy Flanagan, the incoming progressive US senator from Minnesota who claimed her seat after polls showed her in two tight races that she went on to win by double digits, says she has been “underestimated my entire life”.
She was supposedly in a close race during a primary against congresswoman Angie Craig earlier this year. Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor with roots in community organizing, won by nearly 20 points.

articles.title: Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan on her road to victory in Minnesota: ‘I have been underestimated my entire life’

articles.author: Judith Levine
articles.description:
He is responsible for the health of the American people. On his watch, thousands have become seriously ill
At least 11 Americans have died of measles since January 2025 – the month before Robert F Kennedy Jr became secretary of Health and Human Services.
One of Friday’s victims was a child, in Wisconsin, where a baby died of measles the week before. Pennsylvania has not disclosed the age of the other person.

articles.description:
The likely next House speaker has a record of defending corporate interests. His fellow Democrats must fight for Medicare for All and the abolition of ICE
On Wednesday, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be the next House speaker when they take control of Congress. For progressives, that will mean dealing with a powerful leader who has a record of hostility toward the left.
“There will never be a moment where I bend the knee to hard-left democratic socialism,” Jeffries vowed five years ago.

articles.title: Can progressives push Hakeem Jeffries to the left? | Norman Solomon

articles.author: Sanya Mansoor
articles.description:
Cair-Florida is suing state officials after designation meant it had to shut its doors to victims of harassment and discrimination
Omar Soboh, a student at the University of Florida, was organizing a campus panel about Islamophobia when he found out one of the groups being represented had suddenly been blacklisted by the state. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened.
“Our existence itself is political,” he said.

articles.title: This Muslim civil rights group defended pro-Palestine protesters. Then Florida labeled it a terrorist organization

articles.author: Andrew Lawrence
articles.description:
After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement
I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.
Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback

articles.author: Alice Speri
articles.description:
With its policy priorities more mainstream than ever, the left is directing its momentum toward 2028
A week after the US midterm elections swept an unprecedented number of leftists into office across the country, about 600 people joined a Zoom call. The goal: to convince Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president.
On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer with the group. “We are more ready than we have ever been.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fresh off recent wins, the left has a new goal: get AOC to run for president

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it
How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?
I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.

Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme
An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers.
Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP.

articles.title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff

An expert has determined that Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California, a judge said on Thursday.

Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’
The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.
After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

articles.description:
Politicians call attack on independent councillor Ibrar Ali canvassing in Bradford Moor ward ‘deeply disturbing’
Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.

articles.title: Man arrested after ‘horrific’ knife attack on Bradford councillor

Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.

articles.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

articles.author: Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
Four men convicted of sexual assault and rape of Joanne Young, whose husband advertised her on UK swinging websites
• Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years
A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday.
Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

Surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary says he repeatedly voiced concerns and that patients may have died unnecessarily
A senior surgeon has called for a criminal investigation into a Scottish hospital after it emerged that at least 19 patients had died from avoidable complications due to surgery.
Dr Mohammed Habib, a consultant at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said he had repeatedly reported concerns about the hospital’s liver and pancreatic surgery from 2021 onwards and believed dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily there.

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
Reasons to refuse planning permission are limited to ‘public safety’ and ‘amenity’, writes James Ward
In response to your report (Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank, 13 November) perhaps we could start with the harbinger of high-street decline, the digital advertising screen. You know the ones, the pavement-blocking LED monoliths, with screens on both sides broadcasting six ads per minute to passersby.
Even as shops have shuttered, numbers of such ad machines skyrocketed 256% between 2018 and 2025. The ads shown are invariably for global mega-corporations, further driving commerce online, and for unhealthy products such as junk food, alcohol, gambling and vapes (although the latter are to be banned from 1 June 2027). At nearly 3 metres tall and 1.24 metres wide, they contribute to pavement clutter and disrupt sightlines of historic town centres.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Save our streets from yet more advertising | Letter

Human rights committee publishes guidance on freedom of association, which criticises vague laws targeting ‘extremism’
The UN human rights committee has warned against the misuse of counter-terrorism and national security legislation as the UK’s highest court considers the lawfulness of the ban on Palestine Action.
In its first comprehensive guidance on freedom of association, the committee criticises vaguely worded laws targeting “extremism” or “undesirable” organisations.

articles.title: UN warns against misuse of security laws as UK weighs Palestine Action ban

Experts say ‘insanely complex’ £100,000 limit proposed for overseas donors should be replaced by universal cap
Andy Burnham is facing calls to commit to a cap on all political donations when the elections bill is in the House of Lords, instead of the “insanely complex” £100,000 limit on overseas donors. It is uncertain whether the £72m worth of donations recently received by Reform UK will be affected.
The Labour former home secretary David Blunkett is one of many peers to have tabled an amendment calling for an overall cap, proposing a £500,000 annual limit per donor, with his plan believed to have broad support.

articles.title: Cap all political donations, not only those from overseas, Burnham told

Joanne Young, who has waived anonymity, was subjected to years of drugging and rape by former Swindon councillor, who invited other men to assault her
When Philip Young served as a Conservative party councillor for Swindon council, his contemporaries viewed him as a perfectly normal family man with “no edge to him”.
But behind closed doors he orchestrated a systematic campaign of abuse against his then wife, Joanne Young, secretly administering sedatives to render her unconscious, disoriented and amnesiac. Over a period of at least 15 years, he and other men raped and sexually assaulted her in her own bed at their home in Swindon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years

Citizens Advice criticises company for failing to meet Ofcom requirements while reporting increased revenue
Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year.
The postal service, whose parent company was bought for £3.6bn by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year, is meant to deliver 90% of its first-class post by the next working day and 95% of second-class post within three working days according to targets set by the regulator, Ofcom.

articles.title: ‘Pot luck service’: Royal Mail on course to miss delivery targets for fourth year in a row

Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

articles.title: AI demand will push up interest rates around the world, IMF head warns

Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case
Lucy Letby’s lawyer has said the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns.
The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations

articles.author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Latest report also says test-and-trace failures allowed virus to spread quickly and unchecked

UK politics live – latest updates

The lack of international border controls at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic left the UK in an “extremely vulnerable position”, an inquiry has concluded.
In the latest report from the Covid-19 inquiry, the chair, Heather Hallett, also said failures to quickly introduce a test-and-trace system allowed the virus to spread “with deadly speed across the country, virtually unchecked”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lack of early border controls made UK ‘extremely vulnerable’ to Covid, inquiry finds

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

UK politics live – latest updates


The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

articles.author: Mark Sweney

Modella Capital plans auction of high street retailer, which employs about 3,500 people, next year
The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing a deal to buy the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith.
Modella Capital, which also owns businesses including Hobbycraft, completed a deal to buy the 233-year-old business for £42m in June last year.

Similar processes in South Africa and Rwanda have allowed people to ‘work through’ and heal from their generational trauma

The UK has agreed to structured dialogue with Commonwealth leaders after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, indicated he would be open to making a formal apology for Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade. What would an apology look like in practice and what makes for a meaningful one?
